claim: The idea is a two-sided marketplace linking Kenyan farmers with input suppliers and buyers.
text: Founder brief: a two-sided marketplace connecting Kenyan farmers with agricultural input suppliers and produce buyers, focused on validating demand before building.
why: A direct statement from the founder about their own plan. There is nothing external to check.

claim: Farmers will accept a small commission instead of a subscription fee.
text: Founder note: farmers will prefer paying a small commission per sale rather than a monthly subscription. Assumption to test with the first pilot group.
why: An assumption the founder wrote down. No interview, price test or data supports it yet.

claim: Nairobi has the highest smartphone and mobile-money use of the five candidate cities.
text: Household survey, 4,200 respondents: Nairobi shows the highest smartphone ownership and mobile money usage among Nairobi, Nakuru, Eldoret, Kisumu and Mombasa.
why: A large, dated, official survey with a stated sample size. That is verifiable evidence.

claim: Nakuru ships large volumes of maize, potatoes and dairy to regional markets.
text: County agriculture census tables: Nakuru county records large shipments of maize, potatoes and dairy to regional markets, with volumes per sub-county.
why: Official census tables with published volumes. Anyone can check the numbers.

claim: Eldoret is a grain hub with a small number of large aggregators.
text: Grain board administrative data: Eldoret hosts concentrated grain aggregation with a handful of large aggregators handling most maize volume.
why: Administrative records from a regulator, dated and sourced.

method: Interviews with 3 hotel managers, no sample frame
claim: Coastal hotels create steady demand for fresh produce.
text: Trade magazine: three hotel managers in Mombasa said fresh produce demand stays steady through the year, especially vegetables and fruit for hotel kitchens.
why: Real interviews, but only three people and no sampling. A rough estimate at best.

claim: Lakeside market traders show growing interest in digital ordering.
text: NGO pilot brief: among 40 traders in lakeside markets, self-reported interest in digital ordering grew during the pilot.
why: A small pilot with self-reported answers. Useful signal, not proof.

source: Consultancy blog, extrapolated from a 2022 figure
method: One old data point projected forward
claim: Agricultural e-commerce in East Africa could grow 20% a year.
text: Consultancy blog: agricultural e-commerce in East Africa could grow twenty percent a year, projected from a single 2022 market size figure.
why: There is a stated method, but it rests on one old data point. Treat it as a rough estimate.

method: Counted from public pages, not all dated
claim: Three of five tracked competitors run active operations in Nairobi.
text: Public competitor pages: three of the five tracked competitors list active Nairobi operations. Several pages carry no publication date.
why: Counted from public pages, but some are undated. Reasonable estimate, not certain.

claim: Only MavunoHub has a physical presence in Nakuru, and it takes orders by phone.
text: Competitor site plus dated press release: MavunoHub is the only tracked competitor with a physical office in Nakuru, and orders there are placed by phone.
why: Two dated primary sources agree.

claim: SokoLink will copy any new feature within a quarter.
text: Founder blog post: SokoLink will certainly copy any new marketplace feature within a quarter, so speed matters more than anything.
why: A confident prediction about a rival with nothing behind it.

method: Named supplier in a dated release
claim: FarmGate Direct already supplies several coastal hotel chains.
text: Hotel chain press release: FarmGate Direct is named as a produce supplier to several coastal hotel chains in Mombasa.
why: A third party names the supplier in a dated release.

claim: Commission rates in this segment run from 6% to 12%.
text: Competitor price pages: four of five publish commission rates between six and twelve percent. The fifth rate was inferred from a customer review.
why: Mostly published figures, with one inferred. Good estimate.

claim: Co-op leaders in Nakuru name late buyer payment as their top pain.
text: Fourteen interviews with Nakuru co-op leaders: most name late payment from buyers as their top pain, ahead of price and transport.
why: Direct interviews, but only fourteen and self-selected. A solid estimate.

claim: Nairobi buyers will pay a premium for traceable produce.
text: Founder blog post: Nairobi buyers will certainly pay a premium for traceable produce, so Nairobi is the obvious first market.
why: Stated with confidence, but nobody ran a survey or a price test.

claim: Grain aggregators in Eldoret want a digital price board.
text: Anonymous conference chat: someone said grain aggregators in Eldoret would love a digital price board.
why: Second-hand, anonymous and untested.

claim: Most smallholders use USSD or mobile-money menus, not apps.
text: Mobile money provider usage data for 2025: most smallholder farmers transact through USSD and mobile money menus rather than smartphone apps.
why: Platform usage data from the provider, dated.

claim: Institutional buyers such as schools and hotels order weekly and need invoices.
text: Three calls with procurement managers: schools and hotels order weekly, need invoices and delivery windows, and pay within thirty days.
why: Three calls is thin, but they agree with each other.

claim: Several Nairobi supermarket chains and caterers publish supplier-onboarding forms.
text: Public procurement pages: several supermarket chains and caterers in Nairobi publish supplier onboarding forms. The pages show no dates.
why: Real pages, but undated, so they may be stale.

claim: The Nakuru registry lists 38 active produce co-operatives.
text: County co-operative registry export for 2025: thirty-eight active produce co-operatives are registered in Nakuru county.
why: An official registry export with a date.

claim: The lakeside traders association would pilot the marketplace for free.
text: A person at an event said the lakeside traders association would happily pilot the marketplace for free.
why: One verbal comment, nothing written, nobody committed.

claim: About one in five cold emails to input distributors gets a reply.
text: Founder past outreach: of sixty cold emails to agricultural input distributors, roughly twelve received a reply.
why: Real numbers from one small campaign. A fair estimate.

claim: Customer acquisition cost will be lower in Nairobi because buyers are dense.
text: Internal growth model: customer acquisition cost is expected to be lower in Nairobi because buyers are dense and close together. Inputs are not yet measured.
why: The model runs on guessed inputs. Nothing has been measured.

claim: Nakuru has fewer institutional buyers, so first orders will be smaller.
text: Lead list analysis: Nakuru has fewer institutional buyers than Nairobi, so early order sizes are expected to be smaller.
why: Counted from a real list, though the list itself is incomplete.

source: Case study of a similar pilot elsewhere
claim: Co-op partnerships are the cheapest way to reach smallholders.
text: Case study of a similar agricultural pilot in another country: partnering with co-operatives gave the lowest cost to reach smallholder farmers.
why: One documented case, from elsewhere. It suggests a direction without proving it here.

claim: A viral referral loop will cut acquisition cost by half.
text: Pitch deck slide: a viral referral loop will cut customer acquisition cost by half within six months.
why: A slide with a big number and no source.

claim: Ten Nairobi buyers decided on price first; none paid more for traceability.
text: Ten structured interviews with Nairobi buyers: price was the deciding factor for all ten, and none said they would pay more for traceable produce.
why: Structured interviews with notes. Small, but it directly tests the Nairobi premium claim.

claim: Six more Nakuru co-op leaders confirm late payment is their top pain.
text: Six follow-up interviews with Nakuru co-op leaders: all six confirm late payment from buyers as their top pain.
why: Follow-up interviews that repeat an earlier finding. Small but consistent.

claim: Eleven Nakuru co-ops already pay members by mobile money.
text: Updated co-operative registry export: eleven Nakuru co-operatives already pay members through mobile money.
why: Official registry data.
